title: NASA Seeks Industry Bids for First Nuclear Reactor on the Moon
excerpt: NASA asked industry partners Monday to design the first nuclear reactor built to provide electricity on the Moon, a 20-kilowatt system.
content:
NASA issued a final request for proposals on Monday, Nov. 23, asking industry partners to design the first nuclear reactor built to provide electricity on the Moon — a 20-kilowatt fission system the agency wants launch-ready by 2030.

The system, called Lunar Reactor-1, is a small fission power system generating 20 kilowatts of electricity — enough to power about 16 average U.S. households annually on Earth. It is meant to provide continuous, solar-independent power for a sustained human presence on the lunar surface, supporting future habitats, communications systems, rovers and scientific instruments under NASA's Moon Base plans. Unlike solar power, it would work through the Moon's roughly two-week-long nights and in locations that get little or no sunlight.

Proposals are due Dec. 21, 2026. The request is open to industry partners under NASA's Space Power and Reactor Capabilities program, and it incorporates feedback from a draft proposal released in August and an industry day in September at the Ohio Aerospace Institute in Cleveland. The reactor must meet Department of Energy safety standards for nuclear operations. The first task order is to be completed within 18 months of award and includes non-nuclear hardware demonstrations and component-level radiation testing. NASA aims to operate the reactor on the Moon for at least five years after deployment.

Lunar Reactor-1 is managed by NASA's Space Reactors Division in partnership with the Department of Energy. The same division is developing Space Reactor-1, called Freedom, scheduled to launch in 2028, which will deliver three SkyFall helicopters to Mars and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion. The solicitation documents state the lunar reactor will use High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium fuel and respond to Executive Order 14369 and National Space Technology Memorandum-3.

The reactor request follows NASA's Moon Base awards announced Saturday, Nov. 7, at the MAX POWER expo at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Those awards included a 10-year lunar cargo delivery framework with a combined maximum value of $10 billion — a ceiling, not money already spent — with eight companies eligible to compete for deliveries: Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, ispace-U.S., Lockheed Martin Space, Northrop Grumman Space Systems, SpaceX and Voyager Technologies. The awards also included PROMISE, a six-wheeled nuclear-powered rover for the Moon's South Pole, built by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory from Mars rover spare parts and targeting a late-2028 launch for an 18-month mission. Blue Origin received a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million performance option, to deliver the rover on its Mark 1 lander.

“This request for proposals represents an important step forward as NASA partners with industry to establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface,” said Brian Giblin, NASA's Lunar Reactor-1 program manager. “A reliable source of safe and abundant energy will be vital to future exploration of the lunar and Martian surface. Space nuclear systems will provide continuous power to NASA assets in any environment without dependency on sunlight.”

No contractor, design, landing site or contract value has been named. This is a technology-development and testing solicitation, not a finished system.
